brand-deal-rate-benchmarks.html.text:
BRAND DEAL RATE CALCULATOR

Where do brand deal rate benchmarks come from?

Influencer marketing rate cards and creator-economy write-ups routinely quote sponsorship prices as a CPM against engaged followers — cost per 1,000 engaged followers — rather than against raw follower count. That single choice is the most useful thing to borrow from them even if you never work with a marketplace or agency at all.

Why engaged followers, not raw follower count

A brand is paying for a person who actually sees and reacts to the post, not for a row in a follower list. A 100,000-follower account with 1% engagement produces about 1,000 engaged followers per post. A 10,000-follower account with 8% engagement produces about 800 — nearly the same number of real, active viewers, from an account ten times smaller. Pricing against raw follower count alone rewards a large, passive audience over a small, attentive one; pricing against engaged followers does not.

Why the ranges are wide

This calculator's benchmark ranges are deliberately wide — often a 2x spread between the low and high end of the same deliverable and platform. That is not imprecision; it reflects the real spread in what brands actually pay, driven by factors a follower-count-and-engagement-rate calculator cannot see:

  • Past brand-deal results. A creator with a proven track record of driving clicks, saves, or sales for past brands can charge toward the top of the range; a first-time seller usually starts lower.
  • Niche demand. A niche with active brands competing for creators (say, beauty, tech, or personal finance) supports higher prices than a niche with few brands chasing it.
  • Audience specificity. An audience read almost entirely by, say, new parents is worth more per follower to a baby-product brand than a general audience of the same size is worth to anyone.
  • Relationship and timing. A brand that already has a good relationship with you, or that needs content for a specific launch window, will often pay above the general range.

Use the low end of the range as a floor you should rarely go below, and the high end as a target to work toward as you build a track record — not as two arbitrary numbers to average.

How to move your ask up from the floor

LeverWhat it does
Share past brand-deal resultsClick-through rate, saves, or sales from a prior brand deal (with permission) is the single strongest evidence a new brand can act on.
Sell out slots before dropping priceA consistently full brand-deal calendar is itself a pricing signal; discounting an open slot trains brands to wait you out.
Bundle rather than discountAdding a second deliverable (say, a Story mention alongside a feed post) usually protects the per-post rate better than lowering it.
Re-check engagement rate by measurement windowSome platforms report engagement over the last 30 days, others per-post — compare like for like before quoting a number to a brand.

Back to the brand deal rate calculator.

What this does and doesn't do

Common questions

How much should I charge for a brand deal?

It depends on your follower count, engagement rate, platform, and which deliverable you're selling. This calculator applies commonly cited market CPM-per-1000-engaged-followers ranges to your own numbers to give a starting price range for a feed post, a Story, a Reel or short-form video, or a dedicated long-form video.

Why does this calculate price from engaged followers instead of raw follower count?

Brands are paying for people who actually see and react to the post, not for a number on a profile. A 100,000-follower account with 1% engagement reaches fewer real, active people than a 10,000-follower account with 8% engagement — pricing against engaged followers rewards the account brands actually want.

Is this price a guarantee of what a brand will pay?

No. It is a starting point for negotiation based on general market ranges, not a quote, valuation, or offer performed on your behalf. Actual rates vary by audience quality, past brand-deal history, niche demand, and how much a specific brand wants your specific audience that week.

What counts as a Story versus a Reel or a dedicated video?

A feed post is a single photo or carousel in your main feed. A Story is a single ephemeral frame, usually gone after about 24 hours — it commands the lowest price of the visible-content deliverables. A Reel or short-form video (Reels, TikTok, Shorts) sits in between. A dedicated long-form video — mainly a YouTube deliverable — is an entire video about the brand, which commands the highest price because it has no competing content.

vs-marketplace-rate-estimator.html.text:
← Brand Deal Rate Calculator

This calculator vs. an influencer marketplace's rate estimator

Different jobs. An influencer marketing marketplace matches a listed creator to brands and usually estimates a rate only after you sign up or connect an account. This free calculator does the same kind of arithmetic from two numbers you already have — no account, no listing, nothing uploaded.

What each one is for

An influencer marketplace (the Intellifluence/Klear/ HypeAuditor-style category of tool) does something this calculator cannot: it puts a creator's profile in front of brands actively looking to book a sponsorship, and its own rate estimate is usually a feature bolted onto that matching product — something you see after connecting a social account or completing a listing. That listing and matching is real, ongoing work, and if getting inbound brand interest is the goal, a marketplace built around that is better placed to do it than a standalone calculator.

This calculator does the narrower part that comes before any of that: turning your own follower count, engagement rate, and platform into a price range for each common deliverable, using commonly cited creator-economy CPM-per-engaged-follower benchmarks. It needs no account, connects to nothing, and lists you nowhere — you type two numbers your own platform's native insights already show you, and get a number to defend the moment a brand reaches out on its own, through a marketplace, or anywhere else.

It also exists for creators a marketplace often has less to offer: accounts still below the size many marketplaces actively court, where a benchmark number would otherwise mean guessing from a rate-card template found online.

QuestionWhere to answer it
What should I charge for a specific deliverable, right now?This calculator's rate range — free, private, no account, no listing.
Do I need to connect a social account or sign up anywhere?This calculator: no. A marketplace estimate usually needs a connected account or a completed profile.
Will brands be able to find and contact me through this?No — this calculator lists nobody. That matching function is what a marketplace is for.
How was this number derived?See where the benchmarks come from — commonly cited market CPM ranges, applied to your own numbers.
What if my marketplace estimate and this number disagree?Treat both as starting points for a negotiation, not a guaranteed price; the gap itself is worth noticing before you name a figure.
Is my follower and engagement data uploaded anywhere?No. Everything runs in your browser; nothing is sent to any server.

The two are sequential for a creator who wants both: this calculator to get a defensible starting number for free right now, a marketplace if and when getting more inbound brand interest is the actual goal. This page is arithmetic on numbers you provide, not a guarantee that any brand will pay a given price, and not a substitute for your own judgment about a specific deal.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and nothing you type is uploaded anywhere.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or sign up with an influencer marketplace?

Both can coexist, and they solve different problems. A marketplace connects a creator's account to brands actively looking to book a deal, and usually shows a rate estimate only after that account is connected or listed. This calculator answers the narrower question — what should I even ask for — from two numbers you already know, with no account, no listing, and nothing uploaded, so you have a number to defend before you ever talk to a brand or a marketplace.

Why do marketplace rate estimates require connecting an account first?

Because the estimate is a side effect of the marketplace's real product, which is matching a listed creator to a brand's campaign and taking a fee or commission on the deals it books. Reading its estimate usually means signing up, connecting a social account for it to analyze, or completing a creator profile brands can browse. This calculator has no matching product behind it, so it needs none of that — you type two numbers you already have from your own platform's native insights.

Are the price ranges the same between this calculator and a marketplace estimator?

Not necessarily, and neither one is the final word. Both are built on similar creator-economy CPM-per-engaged-follower logic, but a marketplace can weight its number by its own booked-deal history, niche, or audience-quality signals this calculator does not have access to. Treat either number as a starting point for a negotiation, not a guaranteed price — and if the two disagree, that gap itself is useful to know before you name a figure.

Does this calculator list me for brands to find, the way a marketplace does?

No. It is a static page that runs arithmetic in your browser on the two numbers you type in. Nothing is uploaded, no profile is created, and no brand can discover or contact you through it. If you want brands actively pitching you deals, that matching function is what a marketplace is for — this calculator only helps you price the deal once one exists.

vs-the-10-dollars-per-1000-followers-rul.text:
← Brand Deal Rate Calculator

This calculator vs. the "$10 per 1,000 followers" rule

The flat rule multiplies your whole follower count by a constant and calls that the price. This calculator multiplies only the followers who actually engage, using the same kind of creator-economy benchmark ranges — and for most real accounts, those two numbers are not close.

What each one prices

The "$10 per 1,000 followers" rule is a mental-math shortcut, not a calculation: take your total follower count, divide by 1,000, multiply by roughly $10 (sources vary from $5 to $25), and quote that. It needs one number, gives the same answer for a Story as for a dedicated video, and cannot tell a 100,000-follower account nobody interacts with from a 100,000-follower account whose audience shows up every time — because it never asks.

This calculator multiplies the same kind of CPM benchmark ranges against your engaged followers — your follower count times your own engagement rate — and varies the range by deliverable and platform. A brand is paying for people who see and react to the post, not for a number on a profile, so the two only produce the same price when your engagement rate happens to be unrealistically high.

AccountFlat "$10 / 1,000" ruleThis calculator (engaged-follower CPM)
50,000 followers, 2% engagement, Instagram feed post$500$10 – $20
8,000 followers, 15% engagement, TikTok Reel$80$7 – $18

The first row is closer to a typical account: at 2% engagement, only 1,000 of those 50,000 followers are counted as reliably seeing and reacting to the post, so the engaged-follower math lands at $10–$20 against the flat rule's $500. The second row is a highly engaged small account — 15% is well above what most benchmarks call typical — and the gap narrows a lot, but the flat rule still overstates it. In this calculator's benchmark ranges, closing the gap entirely would take an engagement rate high enough that almost no real account reaches it.

QuestionWhere to answer it
Why does the flat rule usually come out higher?It prices your whole follower count as if all of it engages. This calculator's rate range prices only the share that actually does.
Does the flat rule adjust for Story vs. feed post vs. dedicated video?No — one number for everything. This calculator's ranges differ by deliverable because a brand buys a different amount of attention in each.
Is the flat rule ever roughly right?Closest for a small, unusually highly engaged account. It has no way to know that from a follower count alone, so it cannot tell that account apart from a low-engagement one the same size.
How was this calculator's range derived?See where the benchmarks come from — commonly cited market CPM ranges, applied to your own numbers.
Is my follower and engagement data uploaded anywhere?No. Everything runs in your browser; nothing is sent to any server.

A flat per-follower number is a fine five-second gut check before you have real numbers in front of you. It is not a substitute for pricing your actual, current engagement rate once you have it — which is what this calculator does, for free, from two numbers your own platform's native insights already show you.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and nothing you type is uploaded anywhere.

Common questions

What is the "$10 per 1,000 followers" rule?

A pricing shortcut floated across influencer-marketing blogs and rate-card templates: multiply your total follower count by roughly $10 per 1,000 to get a sponsored-post price, sometimes with a range like $5-$25 depending on the source. It needs only one number, follower count, and gives the same answer to every account that size regardless of platform, deliverable, or how many of those followers ever open the app.

Why does a flat per-follower rule overstate the price so often?

Because it prices your entire follower count as if all of it were engaged, and for almost every real account only a small fraction is. This calculator applies its CPM benchmark ranges to engaged followers — count multiplied by engagement rate — not raw follower count, so the two only agree at an engagement rate high enough that essentially nobody hits it in practice.

Does a higher engagement rate close the gap?

It shrinks the gap but in this calculator's benchmark ranges it does not close it. A well above-average, highly engaged small account still prices lower under engaged-follower CPM than under the flat $10-per-1,000 rule — the flat rule overstates less for a highly engaged audience, but it is not built to ever land below what the engagement-adjusted math supports.

Does the flat rule change by deliverable, the way this calculator does?

No — a flat per-follower rule gives the same number whether you are pricing a 24-hour Story or a dedicated long-form video, because it has no input for deliverable type at all. This calculator's benchmark ranges price a Story lower than a feed post and a dedicated video higher than either, because a brand is buying a different amount of attention in each case.
